claims.text: The starting material is a sintered W–Cu composite containing segregated or interconnected W regions within a Cu matrix.
Conventional slow cooling of the W–Cu composite promotes phase separation.
Conventional slow cooling of the W–Cu composite produces interfacial voids.
The proposed intervention is immediate rapid water quenching after high-temperature sintering.
Rapid post-sintering quenching suppresses W–Cu phase separation.
Rapid post-sintering quenching suppresses interfacial void formation in W–Cu.
Rapid quenching freezes in close contact between W and Cu.
Rapid cooling minimizes atomic diffusion at W–Cu interfaces.
Minimizing interfacial diffusion prevents phase segregation.
Minimizing interfacial diffusion prevents the nucleation and growth of interfacial voids.
Preserving a continuous W–Cu interface creates a more continuous electronically conductive pathway.
The more continuous conductive pathway enhances heat conduction under service conditions.
The quenched W–Cu composite will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identical slow-cooled composite.
The quenched composite will have fewer interfacial voids than the slow-cooled control.
The quenched composite will have a more uniform interface than the slow-cooled control.
The intervention must be applied immediately after sintering to be effective.
The intervention is applicable at post-sintering temperatures below the melting points of both phases and well under 1500 °C.
The proposed benefit persists under heat-transfer, thermal-cycling, and irradiation conditions relevant to W-based plasma-facing/Cu-based cooling joints.
The magnitude of the conductivity enhancement and the balance between quench-induced residual stresses and microstructural benefits are uncertain.
